title: Photosynthesis and Limiting Factors
description: Photosynthesis equation, limiting factors (light, CO2, temperature), interpreting rate graphs.
hero_image_caption: Strands of Elodea pondweed release oxygen bubbles in bright light — a living demonstration of photosynthesis converting light energy into chemical energy stored as glucose.
content_html:
What is Photosynthesis?

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and algae produce food. They are the main producers of biomass for life on Earth — almost all food chains begin with a photosynthetic organism. Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light energy.

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction — it takes in energy from the surroundings in the form of light. This is the opposite of respiration, which is exothermic. The word equation:

$$\text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{glucose} + \text{oxygen}$$

The balanced symbol equation: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{light}} C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\)

Photosynthesis is a two-stage process. In the first stage, light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll and used to split water molecules, releasing oxygen as a by-product. In the second stage, the hydrogen from water is combined with carbon dioxide to produce glucose. Both stages occur in the chloroplasts.

Key Fact

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction in chloroplasts: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\). Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll. It is a two-stage process: light splits water, then hydrogen combines with CO\(_2\) to make glucose.

What Happens to the Glucose?

Glucose produced by photosynthesis has several important uses in the plant:

Respiration — glucose is broken down to transfer energy for the plant's life processes. Starch storage — excess glucose is converted to insoluble starch for storage (starch does not affect osmosis because it is insoluble). Cellulose — glucose is converted to cellulose for building cell walls. Amino acids and proteins — glucose is combined with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil to make amino acids, which are assembled into proteins. Lipids — glucose can be converted to lipids (fats and oils) for energy storage in seeds.

Limiting Factors

Three main factors affect the rate of photosynthesis: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. Each can become a limiting factor — the factor in shortest supply that prevents the rate from increasing.

Light intensity — as light intensity increases, the rate increases because more energy is available for the light-dependent stage. At high intensity, the rate levels off because CO\(_2\) concentration or temperature becomes the limiting factor. The inverse square law applies: \(\text{light intensity} \propto \dfrac{1}{\text{distance}^2}\). Doubling the distance from a light source quarters the light intensity reaching the plant.

Carbon dioxide concentration — increasing CO\(_2\) provides more raw material for the carbon fixation stage, so the rate increases. Eventually, the rate plateaus when another factor (light or temperature) becomes limiting. In commercial greenhouses, farmers pump in extra CO\(_2\) to maximise crop yields.

Temperature — enzymes controlling photosynthesis work faster as temperature increases up to an optimum. Above this, enzymes denature and the rate drops sharply. Below the optimum, molecules have less kinetic energy and collide less frequently with enzyme active sites.

The three factors interact (Higher Tier). On a graph of rate vs. light intensity, you might see the rate plateau even though light is still increasing — this means CO\(_2\) or temperature is now the limiting factor. To increase the rate further, you would need to increase whichever factor is limiting. All three must be sufficient for the maximum rate to be achieved.

Key Fact

A limiting factor is the one in shortest supply that prevents the rate from increasing further. On a graph, it shows as a plateau. The three limiting factors (light, CO\(_2\), temperature) interact — all must be sufficient for maximum rate. The inverse square law: doubling distance quarters light intensity.

A common practical uses Elodea (pondweed). Place the pondweed underwater in a beaker with a lamp nearby and count oxygen bubbles produced per minute at different distances from the lamp. As the lamp moves further away, light intensity decreases (inverse square law) and fewer bubbles are produced, indicating a lower rate of photosynthesis.

For more accurate results, collect the gas in a gas syringe or measuring cylinder over water and measure the volume per unit time, rather than counting individual bubbles. Repeat each distance at least three times and calculate a mean to improve reliability.

You can also test leaves for starch using iodine solution: boil the leaf in water to kill the cells, then in ethanol to remove chlorophyll (the green colour), rinse in water, and add iodine. Blue-black = starch present (photosynthesis occurred). Brown-orange = no starch (no photosynthesis). This test can show which parts of a variegated leaf photosynthesise — only the green parts.

The inverse square law states: \(\text{light intensity} \propto \dfrac{1}{d^2}\), where d is the distance from the light source.

Example: A lamp is 10 cm from pondweed and the rate of photosynthesis is 40 bubbles/min. If the lamp is moved to 20 cm (double the distance), the light intensity drops to \(\frac{1}{2^2} = \frac{1}{4}\) of its original value. Expected new rate ≈ 10 bubbles/min.

This relationship is important when interpreting experimental results — a graph of rate vs. distance should show a curved decline, not a straight line. A graph of rate vs. \(\frac{1}{d^2}\) should give a straight line through the origin if light is the only limiting factor.
exam_tip_html: For limiting factor graph questions, always identify the plateau first, then explain which factor is limiting at that point and what would need to change to increase the rate further. For the 4-mark calculate question on the inverse square law, show the formula, substitute, and state the correct units. For the starch test practical, the sequence is: boiling water → ethanol → water rinse → iodine — getting the order wrong loses marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction in chloroplasts: CO₂ + H₂O → glucose + O₂ (using light). Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll. Glucose is used for respiration, starch storage, cellulose, amino acids and lipids.
  • Three limiting factors control the rate: light intensity, CO₂ concentration and temperature. A plateau on a rate graph means another factor has become limiting. The inverse square law: light intensity ∝ 1/d².
  • Practical: Elodea bubble-counting (PAG B5) investigates the effect of light intensity. The iodine starch test shows where photosynthesis has occurred in a leaf.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a raw material for photosynthesis?
A) Glucose
B) Oxygen
C) Carbon dioxide
D) ATP
State two uses of glucose produced by photosynthesis in a plant.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the following (1 mark for any two correct):
• Respiration (to release energy)
• Converted to starch for storage
• Converted to cellulose for cell walls
• Combined with mineral ions to make amino acids / proteins
• Converted to lipids for storage in seeds
[1 mark for two correct answers]

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would use Elodea pondweed to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for any two of the following:
• Place Elodea underwater in a beaker and position a lamp at a measured distance (1)
• Count the number of oxygen bubbles produced per minute (or measure volume of gas collected) at different distances (1)
• Repeat measurements to calculate a mean and improve reliability (1)
• Control variables such as temperature and CO₂ concentration (e.g. add sodium hydrogencarbonate to water) (1)
[2 marks — any two valid points]

practice_questions.text: Explain why increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis up to a point, but then has no further effect.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Increasing CO₂ provides more raw material for the carbon fixation stage of photosynthesis (1)
• This allows more glucose to be produced per unit time, so the rate increases (1)
• The rate levels off when another factor — light intensity or temperature — becomes limiting / when the enzymes are working at maximum rate (1)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A lamp is placed 10 cm from a piece of Elodea. The rate of photosynthesis is measured as 80 bubbles per minute. The lamp is moved to 40 cm away. Use the inverse square law to calculate the expected rate of photosynthesis at 40 cm. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Light intensity is proportional to 1/d² (1)
At 10 cm: relative intensity = 1/10² = 1/100 = 0.01
At 40 cm: relative intensity = 1/40² = 1/1600 = 0.000625 (1)
Ratio: 0.000625 ÷ 0.01 = 1/16 (distance increased by factor 4, so intensity drops by factor 16) (1)
Expected rate = 80 ÷ 16 = 5 bubbles per minute (1)
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a farmer could use knowledge of limiting factors to increase the yield of tomatoes grown in a greenhouse.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (up to 6 marks):
• Light intensity: artificial lighting extends the growing day and increases light intensity, providing more energy for photosynthesis (1)
• Carbon dioxide: burning gas heaters or pumping in CO₂ increases CO₂ concentration, providing more raw material for photosynthesis (1)
• Temperature: heaters maintain an optimal temperature for photosynthesis enzymes to work at their fastest without denaturing (1)
• All three factors must be at sufficient levels simultaneously — increasing one factor has no effect if another is already limiting (1)
• The farmer must balance the cost of providing these conditions against the extra income from improved yield (1)
• Tomatoes produced using optimal conditions grow faster, giving more harvests per year (1)

StudyVault Mastering: all three factors discussed with cost-benefit consideration and the limiting factor concept applied to the practical context.

knowledge_checks.q: Photosynthesis is described as endothermic. What does this mean?
options: It releases energy to the surroundings as heat
It takes in energy from the surroundings (light)
It occurs only in animal cells
It produces heat as a by-product

knowledge_checks.q: A lamp is moved from 20 cm to 40 cm away from a plant. By how much does the light intensity change?
Which test is used to show that starch is present in a leaf: _____
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is Iodine solution (brown-orange to blue-black).

knowledge_checks.q: On a graph of photosynthesis rate vs. light intensity, the rate plateaus at high light intensity. What is the most likely explanation: _____
options: The chlorophyll has been used up
Another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature has become limiting
The plant has run out of oxygen
Light intensity is too high for the plant to absorb
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is Another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature has become limiting.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the word equation for photosynthesis?
flashcard_questions.a: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll in chloroplasts)

flashcard_questions.q: What is a limiting factor in photosynthesis?
flashcard_questions.a: A factor that is in shortest supply and prevents the rate of photosynthesis from increasing further, even if other conditions are favourable.

flashcard_questions.q: State the inverse square law for light intensity.
flashcard_questions.a: Light intensity is proportional to 1/d², where d is the distance from the light source. Doubling the distance quarters the light intensity.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to the rate of photosynthesis if temperature rises above the enzyme optimum?
flashcard_questions.a: The rate drops sharply because the enzymes controlling photosynthesis begin to denature — their active sites change shape permanently.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the sequence of steps in the iodine starch test on a leaf?
flashcard_questions.a: Boil in water (kill cells) → boil in ethanol (remove chlorophyll) → rinse in water → add iodine. Blue-black = starch present; brown-orange = no starch.

flashcard_questions.q: How is excess glucose stored in plants?
flashcard_questions.a: Converted to insoluble starch for storage (starch does not affect osmosis because it is insoluble, unlike glucose).

flashcard_questions.q: What pondweed is commonly used in the photosynthesis practical, and what is measured?
flashcard_questions.a: Elodea (or Cabomba). The number of oxygen bubbles produced per minute (or volume of gas collected) is measured as a proxy for the rate of photosynthesis.

glossary_terms.definition: The process by which plants and algae use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. It occurs in chloroplasts.
The green pigment found in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, usually as light, causing the temperature of the surroundings to decrease.
A factor that prevents the rate of photosynthesis from increasing further, even if other conditions are favourable.
A mathematical relationship where light intensity is proportional to 1/distance squared. Doubling the distance quarters the light intensity.
An organism that produces its own food (biomass) through photosynthesis. Plants and algae are producers — they form the base of food chains.
